utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome back to this courtroom. Today we are going to have the closing argument in accordance with the Rule 86 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal. The purpose of these closing arguments is to give the parties an opportunity to present their views and analysis of the evidence which has been presented in this courtroom in the last 18 months. As it is the views of one party, it is not necessary for the other party to agree with those views and analysis completely. That's why we have these hearings and have these closing arguments. Before we start, are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I just have a couple of matters. The first matter is: On Friday, it would appear, we received a statement that was generated about a month ago in Massachusetts with respect to the events that happened on Branjevo Farm. It would appear to be from the gentleman who was apparently with the 10th Sabotage Division and made no reference to anybody from the Bratunac Brigade being there. Obviously it's just a one-pager. I'm rather troubled that this was -- the interview was on the 25th of August. We received notice of it late Friday, the 22nd of September. Mr. Graham was the one who participated -- that did the interview in Massachusetts. I think this would have been important information for us to have earlier because it shows that nobody from the Bratunac Brigade -- so this would have been important. Secondly, I would like to know if there is anything else out there that might be exculpatory - because I view this as exculpatory - that we are unaware of. So I would ask that the Prosecution inform us or make an effort to find out if there is anything, because I know they have -- their investigation is ongoing. That's the first issue. The second issue is in keeping with the Court's remarks, do I take it that objections are forbidden or discouraged? I mention this only because I have no problem with sitting put and listening to the Prosecution's closing, even though I probably will not agree with any of it or maybe part of it, I don't know. But I doubt very much of it. But I don't want to, tomorrow, when I give mine, for the Prosecution to be all over me. So I don't want to sit here like a church mouse, quiet, and behaving while tomorrow I'm on the receiving end of incoming barrages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for the second issue, I would like to tell you that the objections are not encouraged in closing arguments. Of course, if there is any problem with the specific facts, especially the dates and the number of the documents, et cetera, you may remind the other party of that issue. But generally speaking, the objections in these proceedings are not encouraged and we'll give the parties the opportunity I believe 30 minutes for rebuttal at the end of today's hearing. As for the first issue, Mr. McCloskey, would you please shed some light on that issue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. The Prosecution will continue to provide appropriate discovery to the Defence, especially anything that may be exculpatory as we identify it. And I would expect that this will continue for weeks to come. And if I could go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session and I think it's time for the Prosecution to present its closing argument. I have to remind both parties that we have received the final briefs already. I'm not expecting the parties to repeat what is already mentioned in those final briefs. So try to make your closing argument as concise as possible and please leave some time this afternoon for the other party, especially for the Defence teams to give their rebuttal argument. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Today Mr. Waespi will begin the closing argument with some preliminary remarks and then he will speak mainly on the case of Major Jokic. He will be followed briefly by Antoinette Issa who will speak of the law on joint criminal enterprise. And then Milbert Shin will speak again, briefly, on the law of complicity in genocide. And then you will hear from me at the end and I will speak mostly on the case against Colonel Blagojevic. We intend to finish hopefully today and as you know us, we will do our best to be as succinct and targeted in our remarks. With that I will turn the podium over to Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, colleagues from the Defence, everybody. It's almost unnecessary, Your Honours, to repeat the story of the horrific crimes that were committed by the Bosnian Serb forces after the fall of Srebrenica in that hot summer in July 1995 that cost the lives of thousands. You will recall the testimonies of the survivors of these massacres: P106, the Kravica warehouse survivor; Mevludin Oric and Kemal Mehmedovic, Orahovac survivors; P111, Petkovci dam survivor; and P105, a Branjevo Military Farm survivor. And the other men who were fortunate enough not to be killed. You will also recall having heard from the surviving family members of the men and boys who lost their lives. From all these witnesses you will recall what they said about their own fate and the ones of their family members and colleagues and the events and crimes that changed their lives forever. The shelling of the enclave of Srebrenica, which drove the people first to Srebrenica and later towards a UN base in Potocari. The suffering of the mostly women and kids and elderly men in Potocari herded together under horrible conditions under the eyes of a helpless UN. The separations of families. The moments when thousands of people, wives, mothers, brothers, cousins, friends, teachers and their pupils saw each other for the last time. And you will also recall the suffering of a few survivors, their thoughts and fears before they were led to the execution spots. I'm sure you particularly remember witness P111, the young survivor to the Petkovci dam massacre who was about to become 17 that summer. He was sitting, as he told you, on the back of a truck, being transported to one of the killing fields, recognising his teacher from Srebrenica who was going to share the same fate. I'm sure you will recall what he said, the thoughts he had just a moment before he had to jump off the truck. And I quote: "I got off when it was my turn, but like the others we were all biding our time. We were praying for more time. We were just living for another extra few seconds." And he continued: "Suddenly the lorry switched on the engine and left. As others were killing -- as others were being killed, I was praying that I would be killed, too, because I was in terrible pain. But I dare not call out to them so I just thought that my mother would never know where I was and I was thinking that I would like to die. And I was so thirsty. And when the lorry left I stayed there for a while." Your Honours, you have heard another side, the other side. You have heard the testimony of two of the perpetrators, Nikolic and Obrenovic, who had pled guilty and appeared as witnesses for the Prosecution. You have also heard from other Prosecution witnesses and many witnesses called by the Defence who gave you a rare insight into the mechanics of a crime of mass executions. You have heard from truck drivers, operators of engineering machinery, from VRS soldiers and officers who were present on the ground as the events unfolded. Once, you were also told what the perpetrators did after an execution occurred. They had a nice dinner and celebrated a job well-done. Your Honours, before I deal specifically with the accused Major Jokic, I would like to touch briefly on two issues which were revealed by the testimonies of these mostly Defence witnesses as they relate to the crimes in the Zvornik area of responsibility. The first remarkable observation, Your Honours, from this testimony is the fact how widespread and how well-known these crimes were among the local population. We have to keep in mind, though, what Jovan Nikolic, a former teacher testified about these place: "Bratunac is a small town and all of us know each other well there." And I believe Your Honours, you have taken back the memories and indeed your insight into the locations when you visited the area a few days ago. Most relevant, though, if we look at the situation in the Zvornik area, was the testimony of Tanacko Tanic, a witness called by the Defence of Mr. Jokic, who was an accountant, I believe a cashier within the financial department of the brigade staff in Zvornik. And I quote: "Well, in principle people know everything. You can digress in the Zvornik Brigade and others, but the characteristic thing was that when operation was being planned, it was the women in the village who knew about this first before even the soldiers. So people knew everything that went on and where it went on. So in my first statement I said that there were 7 or 8.000 killed according to what I knew in the different locations Kozluk, Branjevo, or wherever." Tanacko Tanic. Indeed, Your Honours, the killings were no secret. How could it be, given the number of people that needed to be transported, guarded, and eventually killed? Engineering machinery needed to be ready to dig graves, as you'll hear in a moment. We also heard that some prisoners became unruly in the schools so problems arose that needed to be addressed. Other witnesses have testified that killings occurred sporadic even before the mass executions had begun. Bodies were laying around at water points close to public roads. One witness even said, and you may remember that: "The suggestion of a commander that his troops being issued new uniforms if they continued killing. Your Honours, the Prosecution case is that it was impossible to hide these murderous activities. And I would like to address a second aspect which is important to understand. It's the attitude and the atmosphere of hatred that was prevalent at that time in July, the attitude displayed by the members of the VRS and other perpetrators, vis-a-vis the civilians of Srebrenica. I'm sure you recall the testimony of Witness Bojanovic, a Defence witness, a witness called by Mr. Jokic. Like Major Jokic, Captain First Class Ljubo Bojanovic served within the brigade staff of the Zvornik Brigade and was regularly called to serve as a duty officer during some of the days in July 1995. You will recall that he said it was very important to be duty officer and to have experience you needed to have that position. He told you, Your Honours, that he was duty officer on the 23rd and 24th of July, 1995, when his assistant received a phone call in relation to two injured Muslims who were kept at a place called Skelani and made a note in the duty officer's workbook, a book you're going to hear and see a couple of times today: "Skelani have two injured Turks; they cut themselves with glass." When Witness Bojanovic was informed about the message, he wrote down the following in the duty officer notebook, and we can see that on the first exhibit, that's the remark, English translation. Witness Bojanovic said, and I quote him: "I told them to kill them since Bratunac doesn't want to take them." Now, Captain Bojanovic confirmed in court that this was indeed his handwriting, and perhaps we can see the B/C/S version. He didn't say it was a joke. I didn't say it or it was a manipulation. He just said he was carried away by emotions. And he even put it down on paper so it could be picked up by a successor, although he claimed that people wouldn't have believed him, wouldn't have followed it. The Muslims, Your Honours, were even injured. The Prosecution suggests that there's no better way to show the disregard the perpetrators openly displayed against their enemies, now detained, injured, hors de combat. Captain Bojanovic was not nobody, but an experienced officer within the brigade staff of the Zvornik Brigade. The names of the two unfortunate Muslims are known. These two injured persons, Your Honours, were called Sadik Salihovic and Hamdija Delic, and both appear on the OTP list of the missing persons. And we can have a look perhaps at these two. The first name Delic, Hamdija, and the second person is listed as well. Your Honours, what happened -- and that's the second name, Your Honours, as you see on the screen. Your Honours, what happened in the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility was no secret operation done by a few and concealed from the rest. That the crimes were committed was well-known and the perpetrators even boasted about it. I don't need, Your Honours, to touch upon the crime base. You have heard from many witnesses, investigators, Ruez and Dean Manning, about the crime base from experts given partially in writing and they're also mentioned in our witness -- in our written brief with reference to the witnesses and documents. Just picking up from what we heard about Branjevo Farm to remind you, Your Honours, of what Erdemovic testified in the Krstic case, introduced under 92 bis here, that he and his colleagues, 7 or 8 people, alone, on the 16th of July 1995, starting around 10.00 in the morning, finishing mid-afternoon, killed more than a 1,000 people, on one single day. That's the crime base as you're aware of. Let me move to the primary burial operation in the Zvornik area following the crime bases as we have just learned. You know that there were basically four or five primary burial sites around Zvornik for the Muslim men that were massacred, that the graves near Petkovci dam, the school in Orahovac, the school in Rocevic and Kozluk, two sites at Pilica and indeed at Branjevo Farm. And you also heard testimony, Your Honours, that the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade was heavily involved in that exercise of burying, and we'll hear about that later. Dragan Obrenovic also explained to you that it was indeed the job of the engineering company of the engineering unit of the Zvornik Brigade to deal with that. He explained to you that the engineering unit had indeed the machinery necessary to deal with these burials and that the machines were used to deal with it. Briefly talking about the secondary burials in the Zvornik Brigade, you heard testimony that it started around autumn 1995. We heard testimony and presented documentary evidence which implicates the Main Staff, the Drina Corps, and indeed the Zvornik Brigade, including Mr. Jokic, into these criminal acts which were patently open. Let me turn to the accused Dragan -- Major Dragan Jokic. You have already heard how widespread the knowledge was of these crimes that were committed. As you will see, quite a number of the members of the Zvornik Brigade of different units, staff battalions, were involved in all aspects of the operation. The chief of staff and acting commander at the time, Dragan Obrenovic, took the responsibility for it. Dragan Jokic, what were his responsibilities? He had, as you know, a dual role. He was the chief of engineers and he exercised it with quite a substantial authority given and taken by the accused. And he was the duty officer on one specific day on the 14th of July. Now, let me first deal with his authority as the chief of engineers. In that capacity he was a staff member within the Zvornik Brigade. You have heard evidence, documentary, from expert Mr. Butler, from Obrenovic about what the role of a chief of engineers is, an advising role. But he was also there to implement decisions from the commander. In particular, and this is the next exhibit 23/3 provided by the Defence of Mr. Jokic, specifically he directs actions of engineers in accordance with commander's decision, suggests the commander changes and additions in tasks issued to the units. And you'll see that in these documents, I believe on the second page. And, Your Honours, we accept the translation in B/C/S for "directs" is "usmerava" and not "rukovodjenje". But that does not matter, because as you'll see later, Mr. Jokic exercised his duty in reality much more forcefully than indicated in these rules. As an example, Your Honours, we can turn to Prosecution Exhibits 513, the company commander of the engineering companies order of the day for 14th July, signed by the company commander Mr. Jevtic. Here you can see the remark in the middle under item 5, Ostoja Djuric is to be appointed officer for technical service and supplies by order of the chief of engineers. Now, that's one of the examples the way it was exercised. Although the Prosecution doesn't suggest - and we have repeated that many times, Your Honours - that Mr. Jokic was de facto in command and control, it's clear that his authority was bigger than the normal chief of engineers. There are a couple of reasons for it and Mr. Obrenovic explained it to you in court. That Mr. Pandurevic, the brigade commander, Colonel Pandurevic, gave Mr. Jokic more powers because of the lack of military experience Mr. Jevtic showed. Indeed, a Defence witness from Mr. Jokic, Minja Radovic from the engineering company, confirmed that Jevtic had little authority because he lacked military training and had no rank as far as the witness knew. Mr. Obrenovic again: "Jokic controlled the engineers company in practical terms when it came to the professional part of their duties." And, Your Honours, you have heard testimony that the company commander, Mr. Jevtic, was indeed absent on the evening of the 13th of July when he joined Mr. Obrenovic to strengthen defence lines in the southern part of the Zvornik area of responsibility at Snagovo. So Mr. Dragan Jokic, Major Dragan Jokic, the chief of engineers was there almost alone at that level in terms of command of the engineers. Let me, before I come back to the engineers, discuss the role of a duty officer. As you heard, the main description is that a duty officer facilitates the work within the brigade as well as between the brigade and external units. As Mr. Obrenovic explained to you, a brigade duty officer needs to monitor and be familiar with developments in his brigade and in neighbouring brigades, keep his commander and superior officers up-to-date, informed about these developments, and to maintain communications with subordinate units, as well as with superior commands, including MUP and civil defence. We have also heard from Witness Bojanovic how experienced a duty officer needed to be because of the demands given, required by this position. Mr. Obrenovic, Your Honours, also told you that the duty officer could issue orders under certain circumstances on behalf of the commander, and perhaps on behalf of the operations duty officer of the corps of the higher level. And there are, Your Honours, examples in the evidence that Mr. Jokic, Major Jokic, in fact used all these duties, authorities given. One example is intercept P227 between Major Jokic early morning 14th July. He barely started as a duty officer. He talks to General Zivanovic. And you see it on the screen. He says that: "I have information about the Turks." And then he goes on and talks about what he knows about them. There is a similar intercept, Your Honours, and we'll come back to this one recorded the same day at half past 10.00 that night, P233, a conversation again from Major Jokic with a General Vilotic. And as we know from Mr. Obrenovic, that's General Miletic from the Main Staff. And you'll see here that the general, General Miletic, was entrusting Jokic to assist in arranging for the defence of Zvornik. And we see that on second page of Exhibit P233 where Mr. Jokic was told to mobilise everyone and take them up there to cut it off, helping the Defence of Zvornik. In sum, Your Honours, the purpose of the duty officer is to ensure continuous and secure functioning of the command in all conditions. And we also heard testimony of other duty officers. Dusko Vukotic, chief of intelligence of the Zvornik Brigade, also called by the Jokic Defence. I believe he said: "If neither brigade commander nor chief of staff were present, relevant information would go to the duty operations officer first so that he could inform the chief of staff and thus enable him to take appropriate steps in the further course of action." And we heard testimony from a senior officer of the Bratunac Brigade who told you what happened in his area. He testified about the times they heard for the first time about the emergence of the 28th Division in the Bratunac area and when they came across minefields. Then he continued: "That particular commander in the Bratunac Brigade area, informed the duty officer in the operations room that there were voices outside and moans and mines exploding and that was the first we ever heard about any movements, manoeuvres of the 28th Division." You see, Your Honours, the duty officer, usually the third highest ranking officer in the command, absent the commander and the chief of staff has a very, very important function. Now, how did the situation look in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade when Mr. Jokic took over as the duty officer in the morning of the 14th of July, 1995. Now, already on the 13th you will recall, Your Honours, there were movements from the Bratunac area towards the Zvornik area. Transports of prisoners on the 13th already at night towards the Orahovac area. Further, the Zvornik Brigade on the 13th already was contacted for excavating machines to bury bodies on the 13th. We have intercepts that talk about and we have a remark in the duty officer logbook, and that's the next exhibit. I believe it's P133 at page five. To the bottom of page five, it says: "President of the municipality Deronjic called and asked that the flatbed trailer be sent to Bratunac to bring a bulldozer." And at 1000 hours, Colonel Beara passed on the message. There were other activities as you recall. We have a vehicle record of an Opel Record which shows that the military police of the Zvornik Brigade was scouting already sites, execution sites, in the area, and that's Exhibit P510. And moreover, Your Honours, you will recall the change of duties at the forward command post at the night of the 13th between Drago Nikolic, security officer of the Zvornik Brigade, and Major Golic who had to relieve him because Nikolic was informed by Popovic from the corps that the prisoners would arrive. And he informed Obrenovic about that and Obrenovic made the change at the forward command post happen between Nikolic and Golic. Your Honours had information of course from Nikolic about the 3.000 prisoners that were about to arrive on the 13th at night. That was, Your Honours, the situation on the 13th at night, early morning of the 14th when Major Jokic took over as duty officer. Important parts of his brigade whose activities he was supposed to monitor as duty officer were already visibly involved into the murder operation. When Major Jokic took office, he was supposed to be told what was happening in the previous shift, was supposed to look at the duty officer notebook. And the previous officer would have told him what happened. We heard from Milan Maric, another witness called by the Defence of Mr. Jokic, also a duty officer at times. And I quote: "The duty officer would take over the duty usually came in early to prepare, look at the documents, acquaint himself with what happened the previous days, which actions were started, which ones were not implemented, to look over the duty handover notebook to see what was entered by his predecessor." So that was the situation and we believe that there was -- it was impossible that Major Jokic did not know what was happening at that time. But he continued to acquire information after he became duty officer, as was his job because of the 14th of July. First of all, we know that a number of military police from the Zvornik Brigade was active in Orahovac at the killing sites, even senior officers from the Zvornik Brigade staff, coming from Standard where Major Jokic was sitting as the duty officer, left to Orahovac and came back. We heard Gojko Simic, a member -- a senior member of the 4th Battalion who was actively participating in the killings at Orahovac. One of the survivors, Mehmedovic, recognised his voice. At this point, Your Honours, I would like briefly for two minutes to go into private session to deal with one testimony of a witness who testified in private session parts. It will be very short, but I believe it's important for you to put his testimony into context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- yes, we'll go to private session but we have to try to avoid any private session, and limit it as short as possible because this is a closing argument and we want the public to be informed. But we'll go to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness Tanacko Tanic who had been at Orahovac, as he testified in this courtroom, concluded that Major Jokic would have known on the 14th of July about the killings at Orahovac because everyone knew on the 14th of July. In cross-examination by Mr. Karnavas, he was asked: "Do you have reason to believe that this was known to Mr. Jokic?" And Mr. Tanic answered: "I can say in general that on the territory of the municipality, everybody knew. There had been executions, everybody. It was common knowledge. The news got around right away. Everyone knew that executions were going on in Orahovac. Some people escaped and there were problems with the pit and everybody knew everything." Given the overwhelming evidence presented, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that the Defence argument, and I quote them: "There is no evidence of Jokic's knowledge of the events taking place in Orahovac," from their closing brief is simply not sustainable. Major Jokic knew also of other crimes happening in that area. As you recall, witness Pero Petrovic informed him about the prisoners stored at the village in Kula over the phone on the 14th of July. Now, as time progressed, Major Jokic fulfilled his duties in monitoring and communicating with others very well. Intercepts, entries in the workbook of the duty officer, and witness testimonies demonstrate that, that he received and passed on information and gave instructions, all of which were essential to the smooth running of the detention, transportation, and executions. Now, let's have a look at P Exhibit 232, an intercept. And it occurred on 4th of July, well into his stay as a duty officer, at 2 minutes past 9.00. And it's Major Jokic talking to Beara. He urgently wanted to talk to him as we see from the beginning: "Hello, who is it." "Major, I am the duty officer at Palma. I need Beara urgently." And you know, Your Honours, who Beara is from the Main Staff, one of the main perpetrators, as we know from Mr. Butler and other people. Now, he told Beara that Beara needed to call number 155. And Jokic, as you see later, refused to tell over this line to Beara who 155 was. And we know from Obrenovic that 155 was Main Staff. General Miletic again. And later in the intercept, a revealing comment of Mr. Jokic: "There are big problems. Well, with the people -- I mean with the parcels." And Mr. Obrenovic told us that "parcel," that is a synonym for prisoners. In another conversation, Your Honours, intercept again P Exhibit 233. And we have seen that before. Jokic talking to General Vilotic or Miletic as we know. "Obrenovic is really engaged to the maximum. We all are, believe me. This packet has done most to ruin us. And since this morning we have been reporting on the number of people. Well, well --" And so on. And again Major Jokic's reference to packet was a reference to the Muslim prisoners that had been arriving in the area of the Zvornik Brigade in the early morning of the 14th of July. There are three or four other entries of the duty officer's workbook that I would like to discuss briefly. On page 7. At the bottom of page 7. Yes, it states: "Colonel Salapura called - Drago and Beara are to report to Golic." This is a reference to Colonel Salapura, again, Drago Nikolic, Beara, and Major Golic at the Drina Corps, intelligence officer. It shows that Major Jokic was communicating, facilitating communications between key players within those times. You'll remember that Salapura came to testify and he said he didn't recall this event. Another entry, Your Honours, a telling one, on page 9. Again in Major Jokic's handwriting, as was the previous entry. "1500 hours - Colonel Beara is coming in order to Orahovac, as written, Petkovci, Rocevic, Pilica," all known detention and execution sites. Major Jokic is clearly involved in what was happening at that time. Another entry, page 14. "Beara to call 155," and that dovetails, Your Honours, with the intercept we have earlier seen of Jokic trying to reach Beara so he could call 155, the Main Staff. And lastly, page 15, just the next page. Again Mr. Jokic writing down in his official duty officer notebook: "From Beara - Drago to report Mane Djukici. 0900 Beara is coming." And that shows again that Beara called earlier and ordered that Drago Nikolic should report to somewhere. Now, finally the testimony of witnesses who interacted with Major Jokic when he was duty officer on the 14th of July. They also show the involvement of Mr. Jokic into the murder operation. You recall Mr. Milosevic, the deputy commander of the 6th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, who testified that on the 14th of July he was in the area of Petkovci with his battalion. He testified that on the 14th between 11.00 and 12.00: "The Zvornik Brigade duty officer," he didn't know whether it was Jokic or not, but he said the Zvornik Brigade duty officer called him and told him that Muslim prisoners would be arriving at the school in Petkovci. That later the duty officer called back and spoke to his commander, Mr. Milosevic's commander, Stanisic, asking for Stanisic to find Colonel Beara and Nikolic. Milosevic then found them and transmitted the message back to the duty officer at the Zvornik Brigade. So it shows, Your Honours, that Dragan Jokic, duty officer at that time, was coordinating the arrival of prisoners at the Petkovci school. And we have witness P130 who told you that he had contacts with Dragan Jokic to ask him for reinforcements because there were problems at the Orahovac school. He testified he spoke to Jokic and Jokic said: "I'll see what I can do for you." And later these reinforcements came in the persons of assistant commander for rear services, Sreten Milosevic. And it continues, Your Honours, over the 14th and the 15th in the morning that Jokic coordinated, he knew what was happening, he facilitated, perhaps concluding with Obrenovic's testimony on that, when Obrenovic, acting commander of the Zvornik Brigade, returned on the 15th from the battlefield. You know, he was -- he ran into Jokic and Jokic told him about what had happened. And I quote Mr. Obrenovic that: "They had problems with securing the prisoners of war and with burying them." And also Jokic said that Beara, Popovic and Nikolic were taking people wherever they felt like and however they felt like and added that Colonel Popovic had ordered that nothing should be conveyed through radio communication about the prisoners, and nothing should be recorded or written down. And you recall Mr. Jokic in the intercept we just discussed not wanting to disclose what 155 referred to. Now, let me go on to the function of Mr. Jokic as the chief of engineers. I talked briefly about his authority he had, but there was more because he was heavily involved in giving orders to members of the engineering company from the 14th throughout the 17th of July identifying specific excavation machines, machinery being brought to Orahovac, Petkovci, and Branjevo Farm. Your Honours, it's very clear, despite the Defence's submissions that Major Jokic had the authority to order personnel in the engineering unit despite the fact that he was the chief of engineering, a staff officer, and not de jure, the company commander. For example, Milos Mitrovic, a witness, member of the engineering company, explained that the chain of command above him included his platoon commander, Damjan Lazarevic, the company commander, Dragan Jevtic, and the chief of engineering, Major Jokic. And he said he would receive orders from all three of them. Evidence also shows that these three people, platoon commander, company commander, and the chief of engineers worked together. You'll see, and I'm sure you recall many instances, just one on 16th July, Mr. Mitrovic and a colleague were ordered by Major Jokic to go to Kozluk with a Skip type of an excavator, as you know, and report to the platoon commander Lazarevic. And when they arrived they were told to use the Skip to cover the bodies. Now, let me give you the three examples of orders Major Jokic gave to members of the engineers company. The first one Ostoja Stanojevic. He was told by Major Jokic on the 14th of July to take his machinery, a kipper, and report to civilian protection in Zvornik. There he was told to go to Bratunac civilian protection. There he was told to go to Kravica, where he loaded bodies together with other people and put them to Glogova. Two days -- when he came back on the 17th of July, he reported to Major Jokic about his activities, told him what he did at Kravica. And he then asked for leave and Major Jokic gave him leave, which again shows what authorities he had. Second example, Cvijetin Ristanovic, a witness came here also to testify about orders he received. He also told you that he received orders from his platoon commander, company commander, and the chief of engineers. Now, what happened to him. On the 14th of July, 1995, when the executions were ongoing at Orahovac already, he was told by Mr. Jokic to take his machinery, a G700 backhoe excavator, a Rovokopac, as we know, to go to the school in Orahovac. There he was told by another member of the engineering company - I believe it was the deputy commander, Bogicevic - to start to dig a grave, a grave which was prepared with poles, premarked, four wooden sticks 2.5 to 3 metres, and 2 to 2.5 metres wide and about 50 metres long and 1.5 to 2 metres deep. Everything was prepared. Now he started digging and while he was digging, people, Muslims, came on trucks. He was told to go away from this grave, stop digging. He turned around towards the dam, you remember the railway line, and while he was waiting, people were executed. He testified he saw blindfolds, white cloths on these people, these unfortunate Muslims being killed. Later he was relieved by another member of his engineering company. He turned away, went to a water point to refresh. Again he saw bodies lying around, executions, while he was standing there, all on the 14th of July. There is, Your Honours, corroboration of these excavation activities because witnesses saw these machines. Let's look at what we just talked about. Ristanovic came with his G700, a Rovokopac. Let me show what his machinery looks like and it's Exhibit P354, and Mr. Ristanovic identified his machinery here in court and that's his backhoe excavator. Now let's hear what Mevludin Oric said who was present, one of the survivors. He drew a sketch of the machine he saw. And we look at Exhibit P67. On the left side you see exactly the same machinery, a Rovokopac as he called it himself. And you can compare it yourself how similar these two machines are, indeed identical on the right side, by the way, of Mr. Oric's drawing, and a loader ULT-200 which was present as well. You also recall, Your Honours, that while the - and we heard from Ristanovic that executions were ongoing while the machinery was operating - they were even using the machinery, engineering machinery to shed lights on survivors who tried to escape and they tried to shoot them, again using the lights. We have other corroborating evidence which I don't have time to go into: The fuel records for other documents showing that the machinery was indeed active on those days and on the locations specified. Let's turn to the 15th of July. Major Jokic was again involved. Now he was no longer duty officer but he was still involved in his capacity as chief of engineers. On the 15th of July, Ristanovic, who was ordered the day before by Jokic to go to Orahovac, had to go back to Orahovac. This time he was ordered to do that by his platoon commander, Lazarevic. Lazarevic knew exactly what he had to do: Digging, what else? He told you. On that day, his platoon, and two or three other soldiers went to Orahovac. So there were five or six soldiers of the engineering company at Orahovac doing their job. Perhaps one example of the Zvornik Engineering Brigade documents showing what the units were doing at the time is PX521, an order dated 15th July, 1995, signed by Jevtic. That's a good example of what the machinery was doing on that given day. And incidentally the document also shows that days off could only be taken with the approval of the company commander and the engineering chief, Dragan Jokic, at least as it relates to this specific day. On the 16th of July, Major Jokic ordered Mr. Mitrovic, another witness, and a colleague to go to Kozluk, this time with a Skip and report to Damjan Lazarevic, their platoon commander, who would give them instruction. We heard this example before. They also saw an ULT-220 that belonged to a company with the name of Josanica which was, when necessary as we heard, commandeered for the needs of the Zvornik Brigade. So they were using machinery which didn't originally belong to them. They were able to use that. A last critical entry, Your Honours, of the duty officer workbook dated 16th July, 1995, demonstrates Major Jokic's direct involvement in assisting in the burial operation and it's on page 34. It shows that the 1st Infantry Battalion requested a loader. Yes, you'll see now displayed. "An excavator and a dump truck with a canvas to be in Pilica at 0800 hours." The workbook then says: "Conveyed to Jokic and Milosevic." Witness P130 says that he took down this notation and explained that the vehicles were for the burials at the Branjevo Farm and indeed on the following day, 17th July, somebody operated the machinery, heavy machinery, at the Branjevo Farm, and that was indeed Witness Ristanovic from the Zvornik Brigade. On 17th July you also heard witness 178, that he reported his activities at the Kravica warehouse to Major Jokic. Again, he requested leave, to be relieved from his duties for a while, and Jokic granted these requests. It shows how much Mr. Jokic was involved in day-to-day activities of the brigade. To finish, Your Honours, briefly, the reburials. The Prosecution has presented both direct and circumstantial evidence of Mr. Jokic's involvement into the reburial operation. It's basically based on the large scale and the needs, the big needs of the Zvornik Brigade engineers and their involvement in the original burials. It was a massive engineering project in which thousands of bodies from graves within the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility were exhumed and reburied in several graves distributed throughout the Zvornik Brigade zone of responsibility. I believe you heard Dean Manning testify about the different graves, primary and secondary graves which were linked with each other. At least one witness, Your Honours, from the Zvornik Brigade testified that the reburial effort could not have been completed without the use of the engineering units which were involved in various tasks, including sanitisation of the terrain and so on. Milan Maric testified, a witness called by Mr. Jokic's Defence, that he asked Mr. Jokic what happened about the reburial, but Mr. Jokic wouldn't answer him. Lastly, Obrenovic and also P130 testified about the participation of the brigade engineering company and these reburials. And it's just natural that the people who know about the location of the original graves were were involved a second time to take them out and hide them elsewhere. To finish just before the break, Your Honours, it's the position of the Prosecution that we have shown beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused Dragan Jokic was heavily involved in the operations to kill thousands of Muslim prisoners in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. In his dual role as chief of engineers but heavily involved into the daily activities of the company of engineers of the Zvornik Brigade and as duty officer on the 14th July. He not only knew of the crimes but he received and passed on information and gave instructions, all of which were essential to the smooth running of the detention, transportation, and executions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that is high time for us to have a break and we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa, you may start.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning, Your Honours. As Mr. McCloskey has indicated at the outset, I will very briefly address the law on the issue of joint criminal enterprise. I will not, as such, be addressing the evidence that makes out the guilt of the accused as members of the joint criminal enterprise, as that has already been addressed by Mr. Waespi as to Mr. Jokic and will be addressed by Mr. McCloskey as to Colonel Blagojevic. I will address the following areas in my submissions: Firstly, I will start with briefly outlining our position with respect to both accused's liability under Article 7(1) of the Tribunal statute; next, I will deal with three objective requirements that apply to all categories of a joint criminal enterprise; thirdly, I will address categories of joint -- the categories of the joint criminal enterprise and deal with the mens rea requirement for each of these categories; and finally, I will very briefly address the law on aiding and abetting. Just beginning with a brief overview of our position with respect to the accused's criminal responsibility under section 7(1) of the Tribunal statute. Section 7(1) sets out certain forms of individual responsibility which apply to crimes within the Tribunal Statutes. When one of these forms of individual responsibility is of course commissioned, another one is aiding and abetting. Now, although Article 7(1) of the Tribunal Statute does not make explicit reference to joint criminal enterprise, according to Tribunal jurisprudence, participation in a joint criminal enterprise is a form of liability which constitutes a form of commission under Article 7(1) of the statute. Therefore, it is our position that Colonel Blagojevic committed the offenses of forcible transfer and persecutions of the Muslims of Srebrenica as a member of the joint criminal enterprise or planned to forcibly transfer the Muslims of Srebrenica out of the enclave. And this of course relates to counts 5 and 6 of the indictment. It is also our position that Colonel Blagojevic is also guilty of aiding and abetting in extermination and murder. And that of course refers to counts 2, 3, and 4 of the indictment. As for Major Jokic, it is our position that he has committed the offenses of murder, extermination, and persecutions as a member of joint criminal enterprise to kill the Muslims, men of Srebrenica. Turning then to the categories of the joint criminal enterprise. There are three categories of joint criminal enterprise which all share the same actus reus requirements. But the mens rea differs with each category. So I will start with the actus reus categories. Firstly, there must be a plurality of persons involved, two or more persons, in a joint criminal enterprise. Secondly, or the second requirement is there must be an existence of a common plan or common purpose which amounts to or involves the commission of a crime provided for in the Statute. But according to Tribunal jurisprudence, and I cite specifically paragraph 227 of the Tadic Appeals Chamber. A common plan does not have to be a preformulated one or a pre-arranged one. The common plan may be inferred from the very fact that a plurality of persons acted in unison to put into effect the particular crime. The third requirement is the participation of the accused in the common plan. This participation does not need to involve the commission of a specific crime such as murder, extermination, et cetera, but it may take the form of assistance in or contribution to the execution of the common plan. Turning then to the different categories of the joint criminal enterprise as set out in the Tadic appeals judgement. The mental state requirement differs between the three types of a joint criminal enterprise, but I will only address the two types of a joint criminal enterprise that are relevant for our purposes and for this case, and those are what is known or may be referred to JCE 1 and JCE 3, so the first and third category. The first category is what is known as the basic form of a joint criminal enterprise. It represents cases where all the members of the joint criminal enterprise acting pursuant to a common design or purpose possess the same criminal intention. In Tadic, the Appeals Chamber provides the example at paragraph 196 of such a common plan, for example, to kill and says that: "Even if each member of the joint criminal enterprise carries out a different role in achieving the plan to kill, they all nevertheless possess the same intention," which is to kill. So therefore that is the required mens rea in the shared intent in furthering the common purpose. The third category is what is known as an extended form of joint criminal enterprise, and that concerns cases where an accused intended to participate in and further the common plan and in addition to that the accused incurs responsibility for a crime committed outside of the common plan by one of the participants in the joint criminal enterprise, if it was foreseeable that such a crime might be committed by one or more of the participants in the joint criminal enterprise and the accused willingly took that risk. So in other words, the accused does not need to have intent to commit the crimes outside of the criminal plan or the common plan, he needs to be aware of the foreseeable consequences that that crime may occur and willingly takes that risk. The Tadic Appeals Chamber also provides a useful example of JCE 3 at paragraph 204. And the example that they provide is a common shared intention on the part of a group to forcibly remove members of one ethnicity from their region, basically to effect ethnic cleansing, with the consequence that in doing so one or more of the victims is shot and killed. So murder may not have been part of the common design, it was nevertheless foreseeable that the forcible removal of the civilians at gunpoint may well result in the deaths of one or some of those civilians. The Appeals Chamber goes on to say: "Criminal responsibility may be imputed to all participants within the common enterprise where the risk of death occurring was both a predictable consequence of the execution of the common design and the accused was reckless or indifferent to that consequence." I will now turn briefly to the Prosecution's position with respect to which joint criminal enterprise is applicable for each accused. It is our position that Colonel Blagojevic shared the intent and had the intent to forcibly transfer the Bosnian Muslims, the other members of the joint criminal enterprise. And he is therefore liable under the first category of the joint criminal enterprise, of which the common purpose is the forcible transfer of the Muslims out of the enclave. Dealing then with the actus reus, we would submit that that is made out in that we have a plurality of persons involved, some of which are the Drina Corps, members of the Bratunac Brigade, the Main Staff, the Zvornik Brigade, et cetera. They're all listed in the indictment, and I believe Mr. McCloskey will go through that. All involved in the forcible removal of the Muslim population. We also have the existence of the common design in the evidence. The evidence shows starting with directive 7 through Krivaja 95 and other documentary evidence and other evidence that there was a plan to in fact expel the Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. It is also the Prosecution's submission that the evidence clearly and compellingly shows that Colonel Blagojevic participated in furthering this plan to forcibly remove the Muslim population out of the enclave and that he shared the intent to commit the forcible transfer operation, all of which is laid out in section 3 of the Prosecution closing brief. Section 3 of our brief also sets out the evidence that proves beyond a reasonable doubt that Colonel Blagojevic's responsibility under the JCE 3 or the third category of a joint criminal enterprise for the natural and foreseeable consequences of the forcible transfer operation and persecutions, which are essentially the terrorising of the Muslim population, the opportunistic killings and beatings, et cetera, which we say were manifestly foreseeable by Colonel Blagojevic on the evidence. Also the detention of the men in Bratunac, that was manifestly obvious and foreseeable that other opportunistic killings would take place. These acts would be the natural and foreseeable consequences of the common plan to forcibly transfer the Muslims out of Srebrenica. With respect to Major Jokic, it is the Prosecution's submission that Major Jokic is guilty of murder, extermination and persecutions as a member of the first category of a joint criminal enterprise. The object of the enterprise, of course, is to murder the Muslim men of Srebrenica. With respect to the actus reus there is clearly a plurality of persons involved in that operation. Numerous witnesses have testified as to members of the Zvornik Brigade, the Drina Corps, and the MUP, and others involved in the murders that formed these charges. Section 4B of the Prosecution brief and what Mr. Waespi has essentially gone over this morning also provides evidence basically of Mr. Jokic's participation, both as a duty operations officer and his role as chief of engineers of the Zvornik Brigade which shows the -- his -- not only his participation but his intent, his shared intent, in furthering the common plan of murdering the Muslim men. It's also our position that Major Jokic is responsible for the natural and foreseeable consequences of that plan and therefore liable under JCE 3 or third category of the joint criminal enterprise. The natural and foreseeable consequences of the murder operations includes the beatings, the opportunistic killings, and other evidence of that sort, as we argued in the Prosecution brief. Once the murder operation was underway, it is clear from the evidence that other opportunistic killings and beatings were manifestly foreseeable. Now, just very briefly, Your Honours, that address the law on aiding and abetting, it is the Prosecution's position, of course, that Colonel Blagojevic was guilty of aiding and abetting in the murder and extermination under Section 7(1) of the Statute. And according to Tribunal's jurisprudence, in order to be found guilty of aiding and abetting under Section 7(1), the following requirements must be made out. Firstly, with respect to the actus reus, the aider and abettor carries out acts specifically directed to assist, encourage or lend moral support to the perpetration of a specific crime and this support has a substantial effect upon the perpetration of the crime. Secondly, with respect to the mens rea, in the case of aiding and abetting, the requisite mental element is knowledge that acts performed by the aider and abettor will assist or does assist the commission of the specific crime of the principal. Section 3C sub-3 and section 2E sub-3B sets out the unlawfully acts that resulted in the killings of approximately 7.000 men of Srebrenica and shows that Colonel Blagojevic aided and abetted in these unlawful killings. As we argue in the Prosecution brief, the evidence overwhelmingly shows that Colonel Blagojevic did aid and abet the murder operation, and we commend to Your Honour Section 4B as well, in the brief which shows that he knew that his acts were assisting in the murder operation against the Muslims of Srebrenica. So therefore those are the Prosecution's submissions as to the accused's liability in law as far as the law is concerned that I have just outlined -- briefly outlined. And before I sit down I actually would like to very briefly address an issue that was raised in the Blagojevic Defence brief, and that is the test for joint criminal enterprise which is set out in paragraphs 344 and 347 in the Brdjanin Trial Chamber case. In that case, the Trial Chamber basically stated that a joint criminal enterprise requires an agreement between the accused and the physical perpetrators. It is our position that that is wrongly decided, that that is not the law of the Tribunal. To the extent that there's any reference to an agreement in any of the Tribunal's jurisprudence, it merely refers to an agreement between members to further the common plan, which is saying that they share the intent to further the common plan. It is our position that not only is it wrongly decided in law, it simply doesn't make sense to say that there needs to be an agreement between the accused and a physical perpetrator, because not all modes of liability and not all modes of co-perpetration or joint criminal enterprises, if I can refer them -- say that, is a physical perpetrator necessarily required for a JCE to be formulated. For example, it is possible to have three high-ranking commanders who share the intent to commit an offence and they may use their soldiers to implement that offence without telling the soldiers that what in fact they are doing is committing illegal acts. And that is one example of why the Brdjanin test is simply wrong. Stakic, of course, is another form of co-perpetration and another mode of liability which also shows that that test is not -- is wrong in law. In any event, it is our position that Brdjanin is distinguishable on its facts from our case. In Brdjanin, the Court itself distinguished Brdjanin on its facts and I believe stated at paragraph 355: "Although a JCE is applicable in relation to cases involving ethnic cleansing as the Tadic appeal judgement recognises, it appears that, in providing for a definition of JCE, the Appeals Chamber had in mind a somewhat smaller enterprise than the one that is invoked in the present case. An examination of the cases tried before this Tribunal where JCE has been applied confirms this view." And in Tadic, the Court notes or refers to specifically at footnote 890 in the examination of the cases, the case of Krstic, which of course is on all fours with the case at bar, citing that as an obvious place where JCE did, in fact, occur and where it is applicable. So even if we are to go with Brdjanin which we say is wrong in law, it is our position that on Brdjanin itself it is -- this case is distinguishable from the facts of Brdjanin. Also it's noteworthy that Brdjanin did have a much larger geographic location that related to that case and also the time period that it took to remove the non-Serb population in Brdjanin was approximately eight months. The time period that we have in the case before us is approximately four days for the joint criminal enterprise to come to fruition. So it's distinguishable on those facts. With respect to the Jokic closing brief, I note, Your Honours, that in a couple of places they rely on the Krnojelac trial judgement for some of the propositions that they are putting forward. The only thing I have to say about that is firstly, that was a judgement which dealt specifically with JCE 2, which relates to the camp cases that are completely irrelevant to the case at bar. And secondly, that judgement has actually been overturned by the Appeals Chamber and some of the information for which it's been cited in the Jokic brief has actually been overturned by the Appeals Chamber. So in fact it's not applicable. Thank you, Your Honours, those are my submissions, very brief submissions, on the law. Subject to any questions, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Issa. Your presentation is very concise and clear. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I will briefly address the law applicable to count 1B charging the accused, Colonel Blagojevic, with complicity in genocide. The Prosecution has set out its position previously on this issue in the context of a motion to amend the indictment, as you will recall. In short, the mens rea for complicity in genocide is knowledge and not specific genocidal intent. It's knowledge of the genocidal intent of others. In view of the submissions on this point and the Defence brief, the brief for Colonel Blagojevic, we reiterate our position here and we reiterate also our readiness also to answer any questions that may arise on this issue. In their brief the Defence contends that: "Article 4 states that for an accused to be liable for complicity to commit genocide there must be a special intent to destroy in whole or in part a national ethnic, racial, or religious group." That is in paragraph 121 of their brief. In support of that contention the Defence have invoked the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement. The Prosecution submits that Article 4 does not state the proposition that's quoted -- that was just quoted. And secondly, the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement does not support that proposition either. Alternatively, the Defence brief suggests that there is ambiguity on this issue and therefore invoking the principle that ambiguity must be resolved in favour of the accused that the appropriate mens rea is specific intent. The Prosecution submits that there is no ambiguity. The Appeals Chamber has pronounced on this issue and in fact since then a Trial Chamber judgement has followed that reasoning. The Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement clarified an area of law that previously had been somewhat unsettled. In short, the mens rea for aiding and abetting in genocide in that judgement was found to be knowledge and not the specific intent of genocide. And in doing -- in finding that, the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement clarified the relationship between Article 7(1) and Article 4(3) of our Statute. The Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement found that as a consequence there was indeed overlap, specifically between complicity in genocide and aiding and abetting in genocide. It also left open the possibility of differences. However, what is clear is that complicity in genocide at least to the extent it encompassed aiding and abetting in genocide and conduct and mens rea. In that case, the mens rea for complicity in genocide is knowledge and not the specific intent for genocide. In September, earlier this month in fact, in the Brdjanin Trial Chamber judgement, the Brdjanin Trial Chamber followed that reasoning correctly, the Prosecution would submit. In paragraph 726 of that judgement, the Trial Chamber agreed with the description of the relationship between Article 7(1) and Article 4(3) set out in the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement, in particular the finding that there is an overlap of certain heads of criminal responsibility and also with Article 4(3). Consequently, the Brdjanin Trial Chamber found that complicity in genocide can consist of aiding and abetting in genocide, although it is not to be excluded that there may be other acts which are not strictly aiding and abetting but which would amount to complicity. Here the Brdjanin Trial Chamber noted that the Appeals Chamber in Krstic and other cases had held that the term complicity may encompass conduct broader than aiding and abetting, certainly suggesting that it would include aiding and abetting. Accordingly the Brdjanin Trial Chamber found, regarding the mens rea for complicity in genocide, and this is paragraph 730 of that decision: "Complicity in genocide where it consists of aiding and abetting genocide does not require proof that the accomplice had the specific intent to destroy in whole or in part a protected group. Rather, the Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that an accused knew that his own acts assisted in the commission of genocide by the principle offenders and was aware of the principle offenders' state of mind. It need not show that an accused shared a specific intent by the principal offender." The Prosecution observes that in a footnote in the Defence brief, the accused argues that the Prosecution is charging Colonel Blagojevic with genocidal intent and thus was not "candid when seeking to amend the indictment and asserting that it was charging Colonel Blagojevic with knowledge and not genocidal intent." The accused's argument here is somewhat confusing. Had the Prosecution's proposed amendment to the indictment been granted, the resulting indictment would have narrowed count 1B expressly to a knowledge standard. As the indictment stands now, yes, the Prosecution submits that complicity in genocide encompasses knowledge mens rea for sure, and possibly, a specific intent mental state for acts that constitute complicity in genocide but extend beyond aiding and abetting in genocide. However, the Prosecution's position on this issue has been consistent and it's been clear. We are charging Colonel Blagojevic with knowledge, knowledge of the genocidal intent of others and in substantially contributing to that genocide. I would conclude -- to conclude, the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement made it clear that the mens rea for complicity in genocide is knowledge. This is consistent with the jurisprudence on complicity in genocide from the Rwanda Tribunal. The Brdjanin Trial Chamber has followed the Appeals Chamber correctly on this issue. The Prosecution therefore submits that that is a correct law to apply in this case. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't intend to take a lot of your time. We've watched you sit very patiently through over a year and a half of the trial listening to every word and looking at each piece of evidence very carefully. Our case is laid out as best we could in the trial brief and it will be my position today to try to bring to your attention some of the more important areas that I think you need to be aware of and emphasise in your deliberations. To begin with, you may recall my opening statement, you may not, but principally the theme and theory of our case was to understand the involvement of the perpetrators, Colonel Blagojevic in this case. I have always looked at this in three ways, the large picture, the events themselves, the interactions of the individuals, the army, the definitions within the army that regulate individuals, the massive size of this, all the units involved, the horrible, horrible numbers of people killed. There is where there is no silver bullet. This is the case. It is a huge complicated case of inferences to put together to determine what people did, what people knew, and when they knew it. That's the way most criminal cases are. And most cases that rely on direct evidence generally rely on human beings as that direct evidence and human beings are fallible. So I have every faith in circumstantial evidence. In many respects circumstantial evidence is stronger because it forms a linkage, a bond, a chain any number of which could break, and yet the rest hang on. So I have never had any lack of confidence in a circumstantial evidence case, and nor do I have it in this case. But in order to get into the complicated facts and understand what people knew, when they knew it, we are benefitted by the simple military reality of the units. And in this case we're able to see clearly which units were involved, what they were doing. We saw a certain degree of information after the Prosecution's case and after the end of the Defence case, the volume was doubled. You'll see that in the -- in our brief. I think you understood that as the evidence was coming in, as these Defence witnesses took part largely in these events, were either witnesses of it or took part in it. And in any case when you look at these witnesses, they're in a very tough spot. They're involved, they're there, they're witnessing it. I was impressed with their loyalty and their affection to their commander. Clearly they're in a situation where they didn't want to get him in trouble. We saw a couple of times where they actually said something to us implicating the commander and when they come into court they reverse it. But these falsehoods were easy to identify. When they get up and say: I saw no separations for two days in Potocari. These falsehoods were very easy to identify. When they said something else, as in: I was counting and accounting for the men that were separated in Potocari and providing that information on, that's reliable. So I don't think it is difficult in looking at the Defence witnesses and in fact, of course the adversarial Prosecution witnesses in sorting out the truth from the fiction. It's not always easy. It can't be done in all cases, but overall it can be done. And I trust your judgement in doing it. One of the areas I want to briefly talk about that we didn't pay a whole lot of attention to is the area of the history and the lead-up of this. I'm not going to spend much time on it. But as in everything in the former Yugoslavia, history is incredibly important to understand the events. It's particularly important understanding Colonel Blagojevic, where he stood, what position he was in. I'll tell you what I mean by that. When I go to the history I would refer you to Mr. Butler's report, the UN report, and you'll recall the testimony of the -- many of the survivors who first lived in areas such as Zvornik and gradually, as the war began, they were burned and run out of their homes. But that brief history shows at the beginning of this war there was a policy among the RS government, implemented by the army and police forces, to ethnically cleanse certain areas to make an all-Serbian state, as is suggested in the strategic objectives. And this was the way this war was waged. War is an ugly, ugly thing anyway, but this war was particularly ugly because of its ethnic background. So we must look from 1992 and I'll say to May 24, 1995 at this horribly nasty, brutal, ethnic war. No man can go to war and not be affected by it. We know that Colonel Blagojevic was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade in 1992. We know he was a JNA commander. And we know that he was promoted to the command of the Bratunac Brigade in May of 1995. He has to be affected by those events from 1992 to 1995. What we don't know on May 24th is how he reacted. Do you remember one soldier said, a Defence witness, there were honourable officers in this war and there were dishonourable officers. I can't tell you on May 24th which one Colonel Blagojevic was. In fact, I'm not going to get into honour, or goodness, or badness; I'm going to talk about criminal liability. Let's hope he got through until May 24th with some honour, despite his commanders and what was going on before him. I'll just remind you and I'm not going to go over it. We see -- not only do we see events on the ground as set out in Butler's report and the UN report, but we see in November 1992, Mladic's directive, where he talks about beating the enemy. Fair enough. But then he says that to drive them out of these regions together with the Muslim population. We see that same idea expressed in July of 1994 by (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: with his superiors. Then we see the March 1995 directive 7 of President Karadzic talking about making life unbearable and survival impossible. I won't go through those with you. I don't know if Colonel Blagojevic read directive 4, I don't know if he read directive 7. I don't know if he read Ognjenovic's report. I do know and have no doubt, the Prosecution has no doubt, that the result of that expressed policy was clearly visible to anyone on the ground as it occurred. So there is no doubt that by May 1995 Colonel Blagojevic saw this war, saw how horrific it was, saw what was going on, saw the intent of his commanders. On May 24, I don't know if he shared that intent, I don't know how he reacted to it. I hope he was repulsed. But by May 25 the plan to Srebrenica had to been under consideration what was going to happen in July, the March directive to make it happen, it happened several months earlier. So when General Mladic and the Drina Corps appointed Colonel Blagojevic to the position of the Bratunac Brigade, it was clear that this was a strategic position known to them and they needed a man who could get the job done. They didn't need someone they didn't know about, they couldn't trust, they weren't sure of. They needed a man they could trust, a solid officer who could get the job done. I know Blagojevic sometimes appears to be in the shadows in this case because he is not the kind of person that we can see like Mladic or perhaps Pandurevic that will step up, and complain, and make noises. But that doesn't mean we don't get a view of who he is. We do. We get a view of that and I'll go over that with you. One thing we do know is that a coach does not put in a player he doesn't know about for a key position. An army officer does not put in a person in a key position where lives depend on it. More so than lives, which we saw, the history was more important than lives. The VRS went down to Zepa, because of history they wanted to make Zepa theirs. History is important, too. They're not going to risk history, they're not going to risk lives on a commander that they cannot trust. One thing you have seen is General Ratko Mladic is a psychopathic killer. He is the man who picked Colonel Blagojevic. General Krstic, his right-hand man. These are the men who chose Colonel Blagojevic now. Let's not hold that against Colonel Blagojevic right now just because his commanders were that way. But let's see what unfolds. The first thing that unfolds is May 25th, first day at the job, the Drina Corps sends an order to the Bratunac Brigade to shell downtown Srebrenica with artillery, not mortars, artillery. You are aware of the destructive power of an artillery shell when it falls in the habitation of civilians. And that's what happened. When those orders came, those shells were fired. Colonel Blagojevic must have known about it. He talked about it in his daily combat report. No concern indicated. That shell flew into downtown Srebrenica and did its damage. That was a vicious thing to do in any war. This gives us our first indication. I don't know if he's a vicious man but I do know he follows vicious orders. And this was the first example of that we see. Because while you may be able to walk away from General Mladic around a building, and we've seen actual soldiers say they hid from him, you cannot hide from his orders. There's no separate chain of command that hides his orders from commanders; I'll get into that in more detail. When Colonel Blagojevic got those orders he followed them throughout this whole case. Now, we'll get briefly into some of the crimes and try to give you a view of the colonel as we go through it. I keep saying "the colonel," because I want to remind you that that is a senior rank in the VRS, it is a senior position, it is an important position. Now, the crime of forcible transfer as you've heard before and as you'll see and you have seen in our brief. We see that as basically a three-part crime in three parts of a large joint criminal enterprise. The first involves the pressure and the strangulation of the enclave. The gradually cutting off of aid and the various other forms of fear that were -- you've heard about that were placed on the enclave for a long time. That's the first. And in that particular thing we can see Colonel Blagojevic playing a specific and personal role, which I will get into in a minute. Then too is the actual attack on the enclave with the illegal objective to reduce the enclave to its urban area, in addition with what is a legal objective is to stop the enclaves from joining and to stop Oric and his gang from looting and murdering. So this was a two-part attack, one part which was clearly illegal, was not charged in this case. We did not charge every crime that we saw here; we would still be in the Prosecution's case in-chief if we did. It's something that you can consider and I'll get into that in a little more detail. So the first thing I want to go over with you is the 4 July combat readiness report of the Bratunac Brigade. Now, I'm not going to be going through too many documents. I know we've seen a lot and we've seen this one. Because this is authored by Colonel Blagojevic, I think it has particular importance for you to get beyond this kind of curtain of mystery that seems to try to surround the man. Because this is his first major report, at significant time in history. You can tell in looking at it that a lot of time went into this. It's not just a puff piece saying, oh yeah, we're in great shape. It talks about the good, the bad, and the ugly of this report. And this comes from the hand of somebody who is carefully involved in reviewing their command and is intimately involved in its details. And of course, is important because what we've heard suggested that Colonel Blagojevic is the kind of guy that wanders around aimlessly reading maps and that is absurd, as you know, because you have seen this case. I want to first point your attention in the English to page 4. We'll go down briefly through these things and I'll talk about them. It mentions: "The expansion of the brigade's area of responsibility beyond its objective capabilities." This is under the heading of "Difficulties in the exercise of command and control." Now, this argument regarding no zone of responsibility, you've heard it repeatedly from the Defence. You will hear it again. And we I think spent six or seven pages on it in our case. It's such a patently absurd argument that we had to kill it and maybe we overkilled it. I lost count of how many times Colonel Blagojevic himself speaks of area of responsibility in this brief. And we know that there was a map of the area of responsibility on the wall that was referred to and the daily combat reports refer to it. This appears to be an attempt to deny responsibility. And this, of course, Tribunal is all about responsibility. So there is this very obvious effort to push responsibility aside. Even Momir Nikolic was able to take responsibility. We should not push responsibility aside; it's right there in front of us. We go down a little farther. It talks about the great width, 43 kilometres of the area of responsibility. Then on the next page, page 5 in the conclusion he says: "We actively carried out the Jadar 95 combat operation." That's the OP Echo operation. It's one officers didn't want to talk about. He actually was involved in active combat to get rid of OP Echo, had to get rid of it in order to free up the assault lanes for the Srebrenica attack. Okay. And let's look at this almost-the-last paragraph. "The overall combat readiness of the brigade units ensures the defence of the achieved positions and area of responsibility, but reinforcements are needed for the execution of possible active combat operations." He, in this section, is of course, anticipating new combat operations, and says he needs reinforcements for this. This is dated 4 July. He knows Srebrenica is coming and he's reiterating that he needs forces to get through it. Here is an engaged commander that is, in this case, not afraid to speak his mind. All right. And then we get to the intelligence security section. I'm not going to go through the whole thing. But clearly, here is a commander that is familiar with the security and the intelligence operations in his area and is absolutely involved. There is not a secret chain. He speaks of counter-intelligence things. He is up-to-date on the counter-intelligence. He probably does not or should not know all lot of the detail of anything like that because informants and threats and things need to be kept quiet. As the security people said, there is a time to let a commander in and there is a time to keep things quiet. By looking at this, he is aware of the general picture of what's going on. Looking down the third paragraph from the bottom: "The engagement of the intelligence and security organs and reconnaissance units, and other methods of collecting information on the strength, deployment, and intentions of the enemy provides a fund of information on the bases of which decisions on the use of our own forces can be made successfully and on time." He's taking security information. He's taking intel information. He's using it to figure out how to use his own forces. Now, this concept needs to be put into the concept of July 13 and 14 when he was tasked to get people ready for Zepa, for Zvornik, to find the Muslims in the area, thousands of Muslims being abused in Bratunac. This is every bit as applicable to that situation as it was before. He's taking all the situation and figuring out how best to use his troops and to meet the orders of his commanders. The bottom: "The military police platoon has been engaged as planned on the orders of the brigade commander." Something we are reiterating is the military police are under the command of the brigade command. He says it himself. They can't be stolen and hidden and used without his knowledge. Page 8, top of the page: "Three policemen were dismissed from the military police platoon for ill discipline and disobeying an order to take part in execution of a combat task." A couple of things: Military police can be used for combat and not just used for other things. The commander has to be aware of what they are doing at all times so he can use them for combat or whatever else. One. Two, people can be punished, people can be dismissed. There is a way to prevent people from further activity and that is to punish them and dismiss them, something that was never done for the abuse of Muslims, ever. And perhaps most importantly, the third paragraph down, I apologise to the interpreters: "During 1995, international organisations and their representatives have passed through and stayed temporary in the brigade's area of responsibility.
